newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Deal clears path for new European security treaty.
newsitem.headline: Deal clears path for new European security treaty.

text.p: A 30-nation framework deal on arms control marks a major step towards a new security architecture in Europe as three ex-Warsaw Pact nations prepare to enter NATO.

The agreement, reached in principle on Wednesday in Vienna, paves the way for a new treaty next year. It will adapt, for the post-Cold War era, a 1990 pact that set limits on conventional weapons between the Atlantic and the Urals.
"This is an important step forward because it has now narrowed down and given shape to the way the treaty will emerge," a diplomat close to the talks told reporters on Thursday.
"This treaty is an underlying means of preserving stability and reassurance at a time of change."

The 30 states, including Russia and the United States, are parties to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, which limits the number of tanks, artillery pieces, aircraft and other non-nuclear arms the states can hold.
Washington has hailed the deal as a breakthrough.

"In effect, we've taken a treaty that was the product of the Cold War, negotiated with the Soviet Union, and taken a huge step today in adapting it to the new Europe," White House arms control expert Bob Bell told reporters.

Europe's political landscape has been transformed since the original deal in 1990, a year before the collapse of the Soviet Union. Three former communist nations, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary, were invited this month to start talks on joining NATO.

The old idea of a balance between NATO and Warsaw Pact members will be replaced, under the new framework, by a structure of individual national arms limits. These will be coupled with "territorial ceilings", which determine the areas where national and stationed equipment will be allowed.
For example, Germany will have a national limit on the number of tanks it can have and a territorial limit on how many tanks other countries can station on German soil.

All states have also agreed not to increase their current arms levels in Europe, and Russia has said it may consider lowering its national limit to its actual arms level now, which is well below its permitted ceiling.
"There will be no increase in equipment levels in Europe and there is every prospect of substantial further reductions in quantities of equipment in Europe," the diplomat said.

In the seven years since the original pact was signed, more than 50,000 pieces of armour have been destroyed, including 19,000 battle tanks, 18,000 armoured vehicles and thousands of artillery weapons, combat aircraft and attack helicopters.
Russia had been pushing for a revision of 1990 military quotas, arguing that the disappearance of the communist bloc had tipped the CFE pact out of kilter in favour of NATO.
"We understand that this arms control treaty might be a means of giving further reassurance to Russia that this is not something that threatens their security," the diplomat said.
A partnership deal between Russia and NATO in May also helped allay Russian concern over the eastward expansion of the 16-member Western alliance.
However, Moscow is keen for limits to be set to restrain NATO from stationing forces on the territories of the three new prospective alliance members.
The exact details of the territorial structures still need to be hammered out in further discussions in the autumn. The treaty is expected to be concluded in autumn 1998.
The new pact stipulates that there may be circumstances when the national arms levels must be exceeded, such as for peacekeeping, but that this must be by a U.N. or other mandate.
There is also a provision for "specific stabilising measures" to prevent any potentially threatening build-up of conventional forces in the region.
A new clause in the treaty allows for the enlargement of the pact once it is concluded.
